title: Compile a portfolio of evidence for assessment

lessons.title: What a portfolio of evidence is
lessons.html:
What is a portfolio of evidence?

When you do a training course, an assessor must check that you can really do the work. You show this with evidence. Evidence is proof. A portfolio of evidence (often called a PoE) is a file where you keep all the proof together, in good order.

The assessor reads your portfolio and decides if you are competent (you can do the work) or not yet competent (you need more practice).

Kinds of evidence

EvidenceExample in a stable yard
Worksheets and testsYour answers about grooming tools
Observation checklistThe assessor watched you tack up a horse and ticked each step
Work recordsYour daily feed chart or mucking-out list
Witness statementYour supervisor signs that you clean tack every day
PhotosA picture of a stable you bedded down
CertificatesA first aid course certificate

Good evidence

Good evidence must be:

  • Your own - you did the work yourself. Copying is not allowed.
  • Current - recent, showing what you can do now.
  • Enough - it covers everything the unit asks for.
  • Relevant - it matches the task being assessed.

Your rights

You have the right to know how you will be assessed. You may ask questions. If you do not agree with a result, you may appeal. Ask your facilitator how the appeal works at your training provider.

Example: Jabu is doing a horse care course. His supervisor signs a witness form every Friday. Jabu keeps these forms in a plastic sleeve so they stay clean and dry in the tack room.

lessons.title: Putting your portfolio together
lessons.html:
Step by step

  1. Get the guide. Your training provider gives you a learner guide and a list of what must go in the portfolio.
  2. Get a file. Use a lever-arch file or a strong folder. Write your name, ID number and the course name on the front.
  3. Make a contents page. List every section and the page numbers.
  4. Use dividers. Put one section for each unit or outcome.
  5. Collect evidence as you go. Do not wait until the end. Put each worksheet or form in the right section on the day you get it.
  6. Sign and date. Sign your own work. Make sure your supervisor and assessor sign where they must.
  7. Check the list. Before you hand in, tick off each item on the list. Is anything missing?
  8. Hand in on time. Get a receipt or signature showing the date you handed it in.

Look after your portfolio

  • Keep it in a dry, clean place, away from horses, water and feed.
  • Do not fold or crumple pages.
  • Make a copy of important pages if you can.
  • Never let someone else write your answers.

The declaration

Most portfolios have a page where you sign that the work is your own. Read it before you sign. Signing a false declaration is dishonest and can stop you from getting the qualification.

When you get feedback

The assessor gives you feedback. Listen carefully. If you are not yet competent on a part, it is not the end. You get a chance to practise and add new evidence. Ask: "What exactly must I show?"

Example

Lerato's assessor says her feeding section is missing a feed chart. She asks the yard manager for a copy of the chart she filled in on Tuesday, puts it behind the feeding divider, updates her contents page and hands the file back.

Key points

  • A portfolio of evidence is a file that proves you can do the work.
  • Evidence must be your own, current, enough and relevant.
  • Use a contents page and dividers, and collect evidence as you go.
  • Sign and date your work and hand in on time.
  • Not yet competent means you can practise and add more evidence.
